results.title: How can you test the robustness or stability of Sentence Transformer embeddings across different domains or datasets to ensure consistent performance?
results.content: * How can you test the robustness or stability of Sentence Transformer embeddings across different domains or datasets to ensure consistent performance? # How can you test the robustness or stability of Sentence Transformer embeddings across different domains or datasets to ensure consistent performance? To test the robustness of Sentence Transformer embeddings across domains, start by evaluating their performance on diverse, domain-specific datasets. For example, if a model was trained on general text (e.g., Wikipedia), test it on medical data (e.g., MIMIC-III clinical notes), legal documents (e.g., COLIEE case law), or technical forums (e.g., StackExchange). Measure consistency using tasks like semantic similarity, clustering, or classification. Use standardized benchmarks like STS Benchmark (general text), BIOSSES (biomedical text), or custom datasets from target domains. Compute metrics like cosine similarity scores for semantic tasks, or accuracy/F1-score for classification. If performance drops significantly in specific domains (e.g., embeddings fail to distinguish “patient” in medical vs. Next, perform adversarial testing by introducing perturbations to input text. Compare embedding distances (e.g., using Euclidean or cosine similarity) between original and modified sentences—small changes should not drastically shift embeddings. Test edge cases like domain-specific jargon (e.g., “PCI” meaning “payment card industry” in finance vs. Use tools like TextAttack to automate this. paragraphs) and noise levels (e.g., HTML tags in scraped data). Track how metrics like average pairwise similarity across perturbed samples deviate from baseline performance. Fine-tune the model on a small sample from a target domain (e.g., 1,000 legal sentences) and compare pre- and post-tuning performance on domain-specific tasks. If accuracy improves sharply, the original embeddings were suboptimal for that domain. Conduct ablation by removing layers (e.g., pooling heads) or disabling components (e.g., token type embeddings) to identify critical parts of the model. For example, test if removing position embeddings harms performance on structured data (e.g., code snippets). Use cross-validation with datasets like SNLI for natural language inference or Amazon Reviews for sentiment analysis. results.title: Multi-scale detection of underwater objects using attention mechanisms and normalized Wasserstein distance loss | The Journal of Supercomputing
results.content: This study introduces the underwater attention-parallel residual bi-fusion feature pyramid network model, which improves detection accuracy for small- and medium-sized objects in complex underwater environments. The proposed UWA-PRB model substantially improves object detection performance across varying image sizes in complex underwater environments and at multiple scales. This hierarchical and structured feature fusion mechanism significantly enhances the model’s ability to detect and classify objects of varying sizes in underwater environments, where objects often appear at different scales due to variations in imaging conditions. By incorporating this tunable ratio, our NIoU-based loss function enables the UWA-PRB model to maintain high accuracy for medium and large objects while significantly enhancing the detection of small objects. Ablation experiments: analyzing performance contributions, the proposed UWA-PRB model effectively learned feature representations and demonstrated high detection accuracy across different object scales. These enhancements allow v7 + PRB + SPPCSPC\_ATT + NIoU to outperform the baseline v7 + PRB in terms of recall, F1-score, and mAP metrics, demonstrating its superiority for multi-scale object detection in challenging underwater environments. The consolidated results across small, medium, and large datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and versatility of our proposed method, v7 + PRB + SPPCSPC\_ATT + NIoU, in addressing the challenges of multi-scale object detection in underwater environments. These results reinforce the advantages of our UWA-PRB model in underwater object detection, demonstrating its effectiveness in achieving high detection accuracy while maintaining robustness across different conditions. Furthermore, although PRB-FPN-ELAN and other variants such as YOLOv10m showed competitive results, their F1-scores and mAP@0.5:0.95 remained slightly lower than those of UWA-PRB, suggesting that our model’s attention-based feature fusion strategy and loss function design offer more refined and reliable detection performance, particularly in terms of precise localization and classification. Although YOLOv11s achieved a slightly higher mAP@0.5:0.95 of 62.3%, compared to 58.2% for UWA-PRB, our model outperformed both YOLOv11 variants in precision and overall F1-score, indicating its robustness in maintaining consistent detection accuracy across different object scales. The UWA-PRB model, through the adoption of the PRB-FPN network architecture, the introduction of attention mechanisms, and the modification of the loss function to NIoU, significantly improved object detection capabilities in underwater images.
